title: Turn 6: cast Edgar into the alpha strike, or keep casting Vampires?

board.you: Turn 6, precombat main, 34 life, land drop already made. Battlefield: Anointed Procession, Impact Tremors, Sanctum Seeker, Legion Lieutenant, four 1/1 black Vampire tokens banked by eminence over turns 2-5, Arcane Signet, and five lands — Command Tower, Blood Crypt, Godless Shrine, Sacred Foundry, Swamp — all untapped. Six mana available, all three colours live. Edgar Markov is in the command zone and has never been cast.
board.table: Player 2 (Esper draw-go) is at 34 with five untapped lands and has put nothing on the battlefield since turn 3. Stated assumption: a control seat at this bracket that passes with four or more untapped lands is holding a sweeper or a counterspell. Player 3 (Gruul aggro) is at 14, tapped out, with a 4/4 and a 3/3; they spent last turn attacking Player 4. Player 4 (Simic ramp) is at 38 with two untapped lands and is drawing two extra cards a turn.

scenario.extras: Count entries the way the verified lines count them. One Vampire spell cast with Anointed Procession down turns one eminence token into two, and those two tokens plus the creature itself are three separate creature-entry events. Impact Tremors fires once per entry, so every Vampire you cast is three damage to every seat. Verified stack 009 counted exactly this entry shape with three converters instead of one; verified stack 002 is where the doubling math sits on the record. Sanctum Seeker adds one life loss from every opponent per attacking Vampire at declare attackers, and Legion Lieutenant is handing every other Vampire +1/+1 the whole time. Flawless Maneuver costs {2}{W} while Edgar is in the command zone and {0} the moment he is on the battlefield.
scenario.question: Edgar is castable for the first time and the table is one turn from learning what your board does. Cast him and alpha-strike behind free protection, leave him in the zone and turn the same six mana into three Vampires and nine damage a seat, or split the difference and keep protection mana up?

branches.choice: Cast Edgar and alpha-strike behind a free Flawless Maneuver
branches.line:
Six mana, all of it, straight into Edgar. He arrives with first strike and haste, so he attacks the turn he lands.

Swing with seven Vampires — Edgar, Sanctum Seeker, Legion Lieutenant and the four banked tokens. Sanctum Seeker asks nothing of blockers: seven attacking Vampires is seven triggers, so every opponent loses seven and you gain seven at declare attackers.

Edgar's attack trigger puts a +1/+1 counter on each Vampire. The tokens swing as 3/3s, Sanctum Seeker as a 5/6, Edgar himself as a 6/6 — twenty-six power at a Player 3 who is now at 7 behind two blockers. They die.

And Flawless Maneuver is free from the moment Edgar resolves, so the sweeper you are worried about is covered for nothing.
branches.signals:
This is the loudest sentence your deck can say, and the table has been waiting six turns to hear it. Expect every threat assessment at the table to re-rank you instantly.

Player 2's five open lands are the whole question, and you are answering them with a card that costs zero. That is a genuinely good look: you get to present lethal and hold the answer in the same breath.

What the table also sees is that your enchantments did nothing this turn. To an opponent tracking your board, a turn where Anointed Procession and Impact Tremors sit idle is a turn you were not scary.
branches.coalition_risk:
High and, on its own terms, worth it. You take a player off the table, the remaining game is you against two, and the seat you removed was the one racing you.

The rebuild is honest too. Eminence keeps minting from the command zone whether Edgar lives or dies, and if he dies he goes back to the zone and simply costs more next time.

The risk you are actually taking is subtler than the wrath: you spent your biggest turn of the game buying a body, and the two seats you did not kill lost only seven each.
branches.coaching:
Everything in this branch is true. It is also the smallest turn available to you, and I want you to see why in one line of arithmetic.

Casting your commander is not casting another Vampire spell. Eminence mints nothing. Anointed Procession doubles nothing. Impact Tremors deals zero. Six mana bought one attacker and a counter on each Vampire.

The free Flawless Maneuver is a real trick and you should keep it in your pocket: your protection gets cheaper the turn your commander lands. But price what it is protecting. It is protecting a board whose value you declined to convert.

Take this branch on the turn the drains are the kill — when a seat is at seven or less and combat is the only road to them, or when the counter on every Vampire is what makes an alpha strike lethal. Turn six, with a converter and a doubler already on the battlefield, is not that turn.

You are not wrong to want him. You are early. He is the accelerant on a fire you have not lit yet.

citations.quote: The window opens when your win attempt either can't be profitably answered — protection up, table tapped out, interaction counted and accounted for
If a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone.
A commander cast from the command zone costs an additional {2} for each previous time the player casting it has cast it from the command zone that game.

branches.choice: Leave Edgar in the zone and cast all three Vampires
branches.line:
Five mana, three Vampire spells, in this order: Vampire Socialite, then Knight of the Ebon Legion, then Cordial Vampire.

Eminence works from the command zone, so every cast mints a token and Anointed Procession makes it two. Two tokens enter, then the creature enters. Three creature-entry events per cast, three Impact Tremors triggers, three damage to every opponent. Nine damage to all three seats before combat exists.

Then attack with the four banked tokens, Sanctum Seeker and Legion Lieutenant. Six attacking Vampires, six more life from every seat.

Fifteen off Player 2, fifteen off Player 4, and Player 3 is dead at declare attackers without one point of combat damage. Everything you cast this turn stays home — it is summoning sick — and that is fine, because you already spent it.
branches.signals:
Three cheap Vampires read as durdle for about four seconds. Then the table does the arithmetic and you are the archenemy — with the damage already dealt, which is the good version of that job.

Socialite first is not cosmetic. Her own two tokens arrive before anyone has lost life, so they come down bare; then her enters trigger checks after Impact Tremors has fired and hands a +1/+1 counter to every other Vampire you control, those two included. Every token after that enters with a counter of its own.

And you are telling Player 2 something useful, whether you mean to or not: your engine is enchantments. A player who wraths you after this turn is spending a card to kill ammunition.
branches.coalition_risk:
Real, and mostly pre-paid. Fifteen life off two seats gets you named out loud, and you should expect the next removal spell to be pointed at Impact Tremors or Anointed Procession rather than at a creature.

Player 3 dies without combat, so there is no fog, no chump block and no trick that saves them. A kill nobody can interact with generates less resentment than one they watched coming through the red zone.

You end the turn tapped out with thirteen permanents and no protection. Name that out loud and accept it — it is the price of the fifteen.
branches.coaching:
Keep this sentence: the engine is enchantments, and the creatures are ammunition.

Anointed Procession and Impact Tremors do not die to a creature sweeper. The tokens do — after they have already dealt their damage. Damage is not refunded when a board gets swept. That is what makes committing here different from committing a fair board of bears.

Even a counterspell only shaves a third off. Eminence triggers when you cast the spell, and once a trigger is on the stack it stops caring what happens to the spell underneath it. Counter the Knight and you still take two tokens and two damage a seat.

Edgar loses nothing by waiting, because eminence functions from the command zone by its own terms. That is where it has been working all game. The goldfish agrees with the ordering: his median arrival is turn six and he shows up by then in a little over half your games, while a converter plus a multiplier assembles by turn six in more than a quarter and is already down here.

What you give up is Flawless Maneuver at zero. Take that trade. You are buying resilience instead of restraint, and your resilience is a commander who rebuilds the board one token per cast from a zone nobody can touch.

One more thing, and it is the multiplayer heart of this deck: seven drains hit each seat for seven. This hits each seat for fifteen and kills one of them. Your cards should be doing something to all three players at once.

citations.quote: An ability that states which zones it functions in functions only from those zones.
Once activated or triggered, an ability exists on the stack independently of its source.
A creature can’t attack unless it has been under its controller’s control continuously since their most recent turn began.
buy resilience instead of restraint where you can — high toughness, indestructible and regeneration, token rebuilders, threats that replace themselves
Your cards should do something to all three seats or win the game; anything else is someone else's job.

branches.choice: Cast two Vampires and hold Flawless Maneuver mana
branches.line:
Vampire Socialite and Knight of the Ebon Legion for three, and three left over for a hard-cast Flawless Maneuver.

Six damage to every seat before combat, six more at declare attackers from the same six attacking Vampires. Twelve off every opponent, Player 3 down to two and dead to the swing, and indestructible held up for the sweeper.

You pass with a board of eleven permanents and one real answer in hand.
branches.signals:
Passing with three untapped after casting two spells reads as protection held, and that is exactly what it is. Against a competent control player it buys a turn of hesitation.

It also reads as a player who is afraid of a card they have not seen. Player 2 learns that four open lands are enough to slow you down, and that is a lesson you would rather they never got.
branches.coalition_risk:
The mildest of the three today. Player 3 still dies, so the aggro clock still comes off the table, and nobody has to watch you deal fifteen.

The cost is paid to Player 4. The Simic seat drawing two extra cards a turn is the one that wins long games, and this branch donates three mana of tempo to the idea that games should be longer.
branches.coaching:
This is the disciplined-looking branch and it is nearly right. Nearly.

Count what the extra three mana buys: Flawless Maneuver at full price, granting indestructible. Count what it costs: Cordial Vampire, which is three damage to every seat — nine damage across the table — plus two more bodies.

Now price the insurance honestly. Indestructible answers destruction. It does not answer a minus-X-minus-X sweeper and it does not answer exile, and your own list runs both kinds, which tells you how common the second kind is at this table.

And the thing you are insuring is not the engine. Anointed Procession and Impact Tremors walk through a creature wrath untouched. You are paying nine damage for a policy on the ammunition.

The comparison to run is what you lose if the wrath comes now against what holding a threat back costs you in clock. Here holding back costs three damage on every seat and two bodies, and the wrath costs you tokens that have already fired.

Take this branch when the board is the win — a lethal alpha next turn that only has to survive one sweeper. Here your win is already being paid out, three damage at a time.

citations.quote: what you lose if the wrath comes now versus what holding a threat back costs in clock and position

recommendation.choice: Leave Edgar in the zone and cast all three Vampires
recommendation.rationale:
Fifteen life off every seat and a dead player, for five mana, from a hand of two-drops. That is the deck you are holding, and this is the turn it introduces itself.

The arithmetic is not close. Edgar buys one attacker and a counter on each Vampire, and casting him mints nothing — he is the only Vampire spell in your deck that does not feed eminence. Three cheap Vampires instead turn one converter and one doubler into nine damage a seat before you even declare attackers.

The wrath objection is the one that talks people out of it, so answer it with the board. Anointed Procession and Impact Tremors are enchantments. A creature sweeper takes the tokens after they have already dealt their damage and leaves the machine that made them. Eminence rebuilds one token per cast from a zone no opponent can reach.

The free Flawless Maneuver is genuinely elegant and it is still not worth nine damage across the table. Indestructible is insurance on ammunition you have already fired.

So leave him home this turn. Cast Socialite, then the Knight, then Cordial Vampire, kill Player 3 at declare attackers, and put the other two seats on a two-turn clock. Edgar is your next turn, and he is much better arriving to a board of ten Vampires that all get a counter and first strike than he is arriving alone.

You are ahead of your own curve here — six bodies on turn six against a mean of four — and the right response to being ahead is to press.
